name: PRP for hair

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is made by centrifuging a person's own blood to concentrate platelets, which release growth factors. For hair, it is injected into the scalp, usually in repeated sessions, as a treatment for androgenetic alopecia and sometimes alopecia areata.

Small randomized and pilot studies, plus registered trials, have examined it; Wikipedia notes its benefits remain disputed overall and that reported efficacy varies with factors such as number of sessions and preparation method.

paras: Platelets are concentrated to about three to five times normal levels and are thought to release growth factors and cytokines that influence healing and possibly follicle activity.

Adverse effects are generally low in trials. In April 2024 the CDC reported HIV infections in three women who received PRP with microneedling at an unlicensed spa that reused equipment. Use for hair is off-label.

forums.title: Getting Off TRT Due to Hair Loss

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate of plasma protein from a person's own blood, in which red blood cells are removed and platelets retained.[1] Platelets are thought to release growth factors and cytokines that aid healing, though Wikipedia says its benefits remain disputed.[1] For hair loss, PRP is injected into the scalp as an option for androgenetic alopecia and alopecia areata, sometimes discussed as an alternative or addition to minoxidil or finasteride.[1]

A double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot in women with female androgenetic alopecia compared PRP with saline injections, measuring hair count and hair mass index.[2] A prospective study reported that repeated PRP scalp injections improved patient-reported quality of life using the HAIRDEX 48 tool.[3] Wikipedia says PRP was first considered for androgenic alopecia and alopecia areata around 2006.[1]
infobox: At least three sessions about a month apart, then maintenance
PRP not regulated as a drug in the US; preparation devices need FDA clearance

paras: Blood is centrifuged to concentrate platelets, aiming for roughly three to five times normal levels.[1] Reported factors affecting efficacy include the number of sessions, single versus double centrifugation, age, sex and injection site.[1] A schedule described in reviews is at least three treatments about a month apart followed by a three to six month maintenance period.[1]

Adverse effects are generally low in trials, with only weak evidence of harm.[1] In April 2024 the CDC reported HIV infections in three women who received PRP with microneedling at an unlicensed spa that reused contaminated single-use equipment.[1] The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so clinical use is off-label, while devices that prepare it require clearance.[1]

A double-blind placebo-controlled pilot in women with female androgenetic alopecia compared PRP injections with saline, using hair count and hair mass index as endpoints.[2] A prospective study with injections monthly for three months, then quarterly for a year, reported improved quality of life on a validated hair-loss instrument.[3] Wikipedia reports a review finding improved hair density and thickness in both sexes.[1]

Many trials are registered, including an unknown-status study in androgenetic alopecia (n=50),[4] a completed early-phase study (n=30),[5] and studies of PRP combined with low-level laser,[6] compared with secretome,[7] and used as adjuvant in hair transplantation.[8] Their results were not available in the sources reviewed. A veterinary study of microneedling with or without PRP in dogs with post-clipping alopecia is not evidence for people.

timeline.event: Kingsley first uses the term platelet-rich plasma.[1]
PRP begins to be considered for androgenic alopecia and alopecia areata.[1]
CDC reports HIV infections linked to an unlicensed PRP microneedling spa.[1]
